column2: This lamp-flame, the supreme, choicest light, shining like fire, born of the Supreme Self, is the one reached by yogis — thus a lamp-flame for the lighting of the world, born of the king, went (to heaven).
Dharmangada, bowing again and again to the king, said: "All this has been done, father; I shall do your word again.
Sons who do their father's word are blessed in the three worlds. What sin is greater, O king, than not doing the father's word?
Disregarding the father's word and going to bathe in the three-path river (Ganga) — he does not enjoy the fruit of that holy place who does not do his father's word.
My body is subject to you, my life is subject to you, my dharma is subject to you, and you are my supreme god.
A son would not be freed from debt even by giving the three worlds; what then by body, wealth, gift of hair and the like, O Lord?"
Embracing his speaking son, surrounded by many kings, Rukmangada again said to his son:

This is true, son, as you have said, knowing dharma. For a son there is no deity higher than his father; the gods turn away from one who scorns his father.
naradapuran:139:40	I, held by you on your head, son, by protecting the earth, having conquered the earth with its continents and many kings,
naradapuran:139:41	this is the highest happiness in the world, this surely is the way to heaven: that a son on earth be greater than his father.
naradapuran:139:42	I, son, have been made fulfilled by you on the path of good qualities, you who accomplish what is auspicious by making the kings keep Hari's day.
Hearing his father's word, the son Dharmangada said: "Where have you gone, father, having entrusted prosperity to me?
Where did this one, bright as ten thousand suns, come from? I think the Creator, having made her, became disenchanted.
There is no such woman, O king, in the middle of the three worlds. I think she was born of the mountain, or from the ocean,
or the illusion of the demon Maya in the form of a woman. Ah, how skilful is the Creator who made her, Lord! Even a hundredth part of a hair-tip of flaw is not found in her.
She is fit for your house, O lord of the earth, golden-bright. If my mother were of this kind, who else is a more fortunate man than I?"
A necklace of white pearls was placed on the Goddess's heart; a necklace of a hundred palas of gold, adorned with ten thousand diamonds.
The prince then made a necklace lighter for his mother; two sets of sixteen bracelets studded with diamonds for her two hands,
each made by experts for ten million nishkas; the priceless armlets and anklets he gave, the king's son,
to his father's beloved for adornment, sun-bright. The girdle that was Shiva's wife's, bright as fire,
which fell from her as she was terrified in the battle of Taraka, and fell when Kalanemi was established in the kingdom, fallen in Mulapachana,
was taken by the demon Maya, the world's illusionist. Having killed that demon in the Malaya, surrounded by ten million demons,
in a dreadful year-long battle, by his father's order, he obtained the girdle held by the beloved of the demon king.
The king, thrilled with joy, gave it to his father's beloved. The beautiful wife of Hiranyakashipu long ago
had a parting-ornament bright as lightning. When she entered the fire with her husband, auspicious as fire,
she threw it into the ocean in great grief. The ocean, taking it, a pair of best jewels,
gave it to Dharmangada, pleased with his valour; he gladly gave to his mother (Mohini) a thing bright as ten million suns.
He gave to Mohini two lovely garments, fire-purified, a bodice, worth ten million thousand;
a divine garland rich in fragrance and divine ointment, hard to get, from the hand of the Siddha of the teacher of all gods;
obtained by the hero Dharmangada in the conquest of continents, he gave it to the goddess Mohini, increaser of love.
Having adorned her with supreme devotion, he then fed O king, with food of six tastes brought by his mother's hand.
First, having persuaded his mother with many words: "You and I must do the king's word, without doubt.
She who is dear to the king, goddess, is greater than we; whoever acts wrongly toward the king's beloved —
that wife goes to hell as long as fourteen Indras. She who makes co-wife rivalry with the husband's beloved
is tormented in the copper pan for separation from affection; as the husband may have happiness, so the wife should act.
She should do what is favourable and good for her husband's beloved; as the husband, so the wife should look on her, O fair-hued one.
Even serving the lowly she goes to heaven; she who has been dear in mind comes to the later station.
By taking up what the husband desires she obtains all pleasures; by giving up jealousy she would obtain the state of lord of all.
The co-wife who always serves a co-wife, seeing that she is the husband's beloved, has a world that is imperishable.
Once there was a courtesan beloved of a husband in a family of a Shudra caste, very wicked and abandoning his duties.
His wife, who lived with the courtesan, pleased her husband; she washed both their feet and ate the leavings of both.
She slept below both, devoted to the good of both; though prevented by the courtesan she stayed on the path of good conduct.
Thus a very long time passed as she served her husband with the courtesan, in an ocean of sorrow.
One day her husband, foolish, ate buffalo meat with radish and black-gram mixed with oil.
By eating that unwholesome food, scorning the devoted wife, a terrible disease arose in him: a fistula in the anus.
Burning exceedingly day and night, he... the courtesan took the wealth in his house and went.
She gave it with love to another young man, intent on love. Then he, with a pitiful face and shame,
the Shudra, weeping, with agitated mind, said to his wife: 'Protect me, goddess, attached to a courtesan, very cruel.
Nothing was done by me for you, O lovely one, sinner that I am; I took pleasure with the courtesan for many years, O slender-waisted.
The proud man who does not approve of a bowing wife, a sinner, gets inauspicious fruit for fifteen births.
In the house of an outcaste I shall obtain a censured birth. By your insult, goddess, my mind is not stained.'
Hearing her husband's words the wife said: 'Sins done before produce sorrows; the wise who bears them is to be known as the best of men.
That sin was done by me, a sinner, in a former birth; for me, bearing it, there is no sorrow or despondency whatever.'
Having thus spoken and comforted and instructed her husband, the fair-hued one brought wealth from her father and kinsmen.
The chaste woman thought her husband a dweller in the Milk Ocean. Day by day with threefold effort, at night she cleansed his secret parts,
taking the gum from a night-tree (kind of tree) properly, with her nail she gradually removed the worms and leprosy from her husband.
Then she fanned him with a wind from peacock feathers. The goddess slept neither night nor day, O fair-faced one.
Burning with her husband's sorrow, she saw the world blazing: "If there is Earth the goddess, ancestors, gods,
let them make my husband free of disease, free of sin. I shall give to Chandika the blood and flesh,
with man, goat, buffalo, for my husband's health. With respect I shall have done ten fasts.
I shall lay my body on a bed of fine thorns; I shall not eat sweet things nor ghee,
I shall remain for a heap of days without outer anointing; may my husband be disease-free and live a hundred autumns."
Speaking so as day after day passed, in a short time his three humours became disordered.
She gave her husband the Trikatu with great care; shivering with cold, he bit off her finger.
Between the two bitten, a clasp suddenly occurred; the piece from her finger stayed in his mouth, O king's beloved.
Then selling her bracelet and buying much wood, she made a pyre with ghee and placed her husband in the middle.
Descending, she took the fire with her arms and drew it with her foot; placing mouth on mouth, heart on heart,
and hip on hip, goddess, setting herself on him, the auspicious one burned her husband's diseased body.
The fair-limbed one burned with herself, in the blazing fire.
Casting off her body, she suddenly went with her husband to the world of the gods, having purified a heap of sins by her own deed and hard accomplishment."
The goddess, sitting on a lovely golden seat, being fanned with a fine fan, singing well,
by Dharmangada's... with a fan made of peacock tails, the daughter of Brahma ate that food, like nectar.
Having cleaned herself with water cold fourfold, she took the fragrant betel given by her son.
With a hand smeared with fine sandal, the fair-hued one then slowly laughed and said to Sandhyavali, O king:
Goddess, are you the mother of King Vrishangada? I did not know, fair one, being sweating with fatigue.
While the daughter of Brahma spoke so to Sandhyavali, O king, the king's son bowed and said:

By this goddess I was carried in the womb for three years; by your husband's grace I have grown.
naradapuran:141:25	I have many hundreds of mothers, fair one; but of her I drank much milk, soaked in affection, from her breasts.
naradapuran:141:26	By her, severe pain and old age were mostly borne; having borne me she became loose in her bonds.
naradapuran:141:27	There is nothing in the three worlds, fair-limbed one, by giving which a son would be free of debt to his mother; this I say truly.
naradapuran:141:28	I am the most fortunate in the world; no man is greater than I. I shall always keep to the lap of the company of mothers.
naradapuran:141:29	If a son does not sit in the lap of his mother, he does not know a mother's happiness, as a girl does not know her husband's.
naradapuran:141:30	A son who has climbed to his mother's lap becomes proud; he wishes to take with his hand the necklace on her fine body.
naradapuran:141:31	Cared for by his mother, even a fatherless son becomes proud; he wishes to sustain the world, drinking vigorous mother's milk.
naradapuran:141:32	This one, joined with the womb, is anxious about the lap. If there is no difference between her and the others for me,
naradapuran:141:33	by that truth may my father live a hundred autumns. While the son spoke so, Mohini was amazed.

How can I harm him, I of pitiless nature? It is improper in the house of a sinner for a disciplined, sinless one.
naradapuran:141:35	One who serves his father has no equal on earth. To do a censured deed to one greater in virtue,
naradapuran:141:36	to a righteous son, being his mother on earth... Thus pondering in many ways, Mohini, beauty of the world,
said to her son, the girl: "Quickly bring my husband; I cannot stay even a moment without him."
Then he went quickly, bowed to his father, and said: "Father, the youngest mother wishes to see you quickly.
Show her favour; the daughter of Brahma is to be honoured." At the son's words the king was ready to go that very moment.
With a glad face he entered Sandhyavali's house; entering the house, the king saw her lying on the bed:
Mohini, deluded, bright as heated gold. Worshipping the pride of his beloved Sandhyavali slowly,
setting aside his anger at his co-wife's rivalry at the son's word, and seeing Rukmangada arrived, the fair one, bewildering him on the bed,
with a glad face said to the king of abundant gifts: "Sit here, beloved, on the soft-cushioned couch.
The government of the kingdom has long been seen by you, O king; even today your wish does not turn back from the kingdom.
I think you a doer of evil on this earth, who knowing a son capable, yourself looks after the kingly wealth.
Therefore no one in the worlds is more unhappy than you; the happiness of fathers with good sons is for a moment, O king,
through the pain of sinners enjoying, with minds attached to objects. All your subjects, O king, dear, born of complete merit,
while Dharmangada is ruling, how do you look on now? Giving up the happiness of the beloved, like a weak farmer?
If you protect the kingdom, what use am I to you? I was brought needlessly from the head of the Milk Ocean.
I shall become food for vultures, like prey of birds. Whoever here, ill-minded, does not serve his young wife,
devoted to business — whence will he have a beloved? A wife unserved goes, wealth not given goes,
an unguarded kingdom goes, unpractised learning goes. Learning is not gained by the lazy, nor a wife by those firm in vows;
without practice there is no prosperity; fame is not gained by the undevoted; the diligent get happiness; one without a wife gets no offspring;
an impure man does not obtain dharma, nor a Brahmin of harsh speech wealth; one does not know without asking, nor go anywhere without going.
An undisciplined man does not know rites; a sleeper does not know fear. Why, O king, leaving me, in the auspicious house of Dharmangada,
do you look on the kingdom's station, when your son is capable?"
To his daughter-in-law-like (Mohini) thus speaking, the beloved of Rati, with lovely wide eyes, the king, ashamed, standing near his son, said to his beloved:

Better that all your mothers die at once, son, than that a husband be seen with his own eyes in attachment to another woman.
naradapuran:142:25	But this king, the husband, should not be seen joined with Mohini. Dharmangada said: "If you, fair-faced ones, will not give my father happiness,
I shall drink a stirred poison; your happiness is when I am dead. Whoever by deed, mind or speech causes my father pain,
she is my enemy, to be killed, even if she be Sandhyavali. The goddess Mohini, dear to my father, is superior to all,
a girl who has come to play from the palace on Mount Mandara." Hearing her son's words, the mothers, trembling,
said with choked voice for the good of their son: "Your word must be done, justly.
But let your father go to Mohini after giving gifts. A husband who marries a second or another wife
should give the elder wife twice her share, otherwise he is in debt. When the husband, having taken leave, marries another younger one,
then the elder's wish must be given, say the ancients. The best of men should do sacrifice and merit-works with the elder.
This is dharma; otherwise injustice arises and dharma is destroyed." Hearing his mothers' words, delighted in heart,
the son gave each a full ten million; and gave a thousand cities and villages.
The king's son gave to each, with four mules each, eight golden-garlanded chariots,
gave ten thousand garments worth a hundred more, and of pure imperishable gold from Meru, the king's son
gave a hundred thousand to each mother. He gave a hundred male slaves and a hundred maid-servants,
ten thousand cows each giving a pot of milk, and a thousand good strong draught-oxen to each.
O king, the son gave grain of ten kinds, and a hundred thousand gardens, as if laughing.
He gave ten thousand pots of ghee and of oil separately, and countless goats and sheep to each.
With a thousand thousand gold ornaments he adorned them, devoted, with Indra's weapon-bright ornaments,
with pearls shining, the size of amalaka fruit, joined together as five or seven bracelets;
five thousand and two hundred pearls, bright as the moon, he gave Sandhyavali here.
To each he gave a lovely pair of necklaces; saffron, sandal and camphor in prasthas in abundance,
and musk in plenty the son gave them, to all mothers alike, wishing his father's happiness.
Variegated vessels, many water-vessels, vessels of ghee and milk and various drinks,
fourteen hundred and a thousand golden dishes with pots the prince gave;
to each, O king, three hundred and five elephants (cows?) of swift speed and broad shoulders,
twenty each, and a hundred she-camels each; palanquins with bearers and strong-limbed men,
he gave seven horses to the mothers going comfortably. Having thus given much wealth to the many, the king's son,
blessed, like the lord of wealth, circumambulated them, and with folded hands said this:

At my request, I bow my head to you; as you are, saying of the husband: 'Let all of you tell my father today: enjoy the king with Mohini at will.
naradapuran:142:53	Let there be no jealousy of us in your mind, even a little. Delight with the pure daughter of Brahma, good-natured Mohini, in happiness in secret for hundreds of times.'
Hearing the son's words, all of them, their hair standing on end with joy, said to the king: "Delight long with the daughter of the self-born, as the hero of Raghu with Videha's daughter.
The daughter of Kushaketu is no thorn in our side; by your union, certainly, we have no doubt. By your son's might, freed from sorrow, accept this speech told."
Enjoying pleasures, people go to Hari's abode by serving that day. On dark nights, O king, they make the doors secure, not afraid of robbers.
Nor do they give a livelihood to cowherds; wandering at will they come to the house. The cows, dripping milk like pots, very many, fond of calves, bring peace.
